title: Math Refresher
subtitle: Linear Algebra, Calculus & Probability for ML (Optional)
content:
🎯 What You'll Be Able to Do

  • Read the math in deep-learning and quantum-ML lessons without panic
  • Understand vectors, matrices, dot products, and why they matter for ML
  • Understand derivatives as "how much the output moves when an input moves"
  • Understand probability distributions, expectation, and variance

Before you start: High-school algebra. This lesson is optional - skip it if you already know what a derivative and a covariance matrix are.

How to use this lesson: skim each section, and only stop where a concept is unfamiliar. You don't need to memorize formulas - you need to recognize what they represent.

📐 Linear Algebra — Vectors and Matrices

Vector — an ordered list of numbers, e.g. x = [1.2, -0.4, 3.0] in R^3. Geometrically: a point or a direction in space.

Matrix — a 2D grid of numbers. A matrix A (m x n) maps an n-vector to an m-vector via Ax.

Dot product: a . b = sum(a_i * b_i). It's the building block of neural layers (w . x + b) and similarity (cosine similarity).

Matrix multiplication: composition. If B maps n-vectors to m-vectors and A maps m-vectors to k-vectors, then A(Bx) = (AB)x is a k-vector.

Eigenvalues / eigenvectors: the directions v that don't rotate under A, only scale: Av = lambda * v. Intuition: special directions where the matrix acts like a single number.

Why this matters for ML: a neural network layer y = Wx + b is a matrix-vector product plus a bias. Backpropagation is purely matrix calculus.

# NumPy: the lingua franca of ML math
import numpy as np
v = np.array([1.2, -0.4, 3.0])  # a vector in R^3
M = np.array([[1, 2, 0], [0, 1, 4]])  # 2x3 matrix
y = M @ v  # y in R^2
print(y, y.shape)  # [1.2, 11.6] (2,)
print(v @ v)  # dot product

📉 Calculus — Derivatives and Gradients

Derivative — df/dx is "how much the output moves when x moves". f(x) = x^2 -> df/dx = 2x (at x=3, slope is 6).

Partial derivative — derivative of f(x_1, ..., x_n) w.r.t. one variable, holding others fixed. Written partial f / partial x_i.

Gradient — vector of all partials. grad f = [df/dx_1, ..., df/dx_n]. It points in the direction of steepest ascent.

Training loop in one line: w = w - lr * grad L — go downhill, where lr (learning rate) is the step size. That's gradient descent.

Chain rule: d f(g(x)) / dx = (df/dg) * (dg/dx). Backprop is just the chain rule applied layer-by-layer.

Why this matters for ML: training = minimizing a loss function. We use gradients to know which direction is downhill.

🎲 Probability — Distributions, Expectation, Variance

Random variable (RV) — a variable whose value is uncertain. Can be discrete (coin toss) or continuous (height).

Probability distribution: how likely each value is.

  • Discrete: probability mass function p(x) = P(X=x).
  • Continuous: probability density function p(x); the area under p is 1.

Expectation E[X] = sum x * p(x) (or integral for continuous). The long-run average.

Variance Var(X) = E[(X - E[X])^2] — how spread out the values are.

Conditional probability P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B). Bayes' rule flips conditions: P(A|B) = P(B|A) P(A) / P(B).

Why this matters for ML: classification is "estimate P(class | input)". Generative models (LLMs) model P(token | previous tokens). Across the whole course you'll see softmax(x)_i = exp(x_i) / sum_j exp(x_j) — a probability distribution over classes/tokens.

🧠 Tying it Together — softmax in One Line

One formula that uses everything above:

softmax(z)_i = exp(z_i) / sum_j exp(z_j)
  • Takes a vector z (linear algebra)
  • Its derivative is clean (calculus: d softmax/dz = softmax - softmax * softmax)
  • Outputs a probability distribution that sums to 1 (probability)

Softmax is the output layer for classification; cross-entropy loss is the matching training objective. Together they make neural-network classifier training work.

questions.question: A neural network layer computes y = Wx + b. In shape terms, if x is in R^n and y is in R^m, what is W?

options.text: An m x n matrix (it maps an n-vector to an m-vector)

questions.explanation: Ax maps n-vectors to m-vectors only when A has m rows and n columns. The bias b is added elementwise after, so it's also in R^m.

questions.question: The gradient grad L points in the direction of steepest ascent of L. Why do we train with w = w - lr * grad L?

options.text: The minus sign flips the direction, so we move downhill (steapest descent), minimizing L
We want to maximize L, and the minus sign is a bug
It doesn't - we use plus, not minus

questions.explanation: Gradient descent moves opposite the gradient (downhill) by step size lr. Gradient ascent uses plus.

questions.question: EF[X] = sum x*p(x). What does expectation represent intuitively?

options.text: The long-run average value of X
The most likely value of X

questions.explanation: Expectation is the long-run average. The most likely value (mode) and the maximum are different things and may not equal E[X].

questions.question: Backpropagation is essentially which math tool applied repeatedly?
questions.explanation: Backprop is the chain rule applied layer-by-layer to compute gradients of the loss w.r.t. every weight.

questions.question: softmax(z)_i = exp(z_i) / sum_j exp(z_j). Why does the denominator sum over all j?

options.text: So the output is a probability distribution that sums to 1
To avoid a division-by-zero error on diagonal elements

questions.explanation: The denominator normalizes the exponentiated scores so the output sums to 1, making it valid as a categorical probability.
